title: Pillar I — React & the UI Rendering Engine

sections.heading: Components, props, and state
paragraphs: A React component is a function that takes props and returns a description of UI. Props flow down from parent to child and are read-only. State is a component's own memory, created with `useState`, and changing it is what triggers a re-render.

The golden rule: never mutate state directly. `items.push(x)` changes the array in place — React compares references, sees the same array, and skips the re-render. `setItems([...items, x])` creates a new reference React can detect.

Think of every render as a photograph: the component function runs top to bottom with that moment's props and state, producing a fresh snapshot of the UI. Each render's props and state are frozen for that render — a value you read won't change out from under you mid-function, which is why closures inside a render 'see' that render's values.
sections.summary: To update state, make a fresh copy instead of changing it in place, or React won't notice and won't re-render. Props flow down and are read-only; state is local and immutable-by-convention.

variants.question: A developer writes `user.name = 'Ada'; setUser(user);` but the component doesn't re-render. Why?
options: useState refuses to hold objects that carry nested properties like this
setUser accepts only string values and silently rejects any object
The object was mutated in place, so its reference stays the same and React bails
React is batching the change internally, and it only appears after a full page refresh
variants.rationale: React uses Object.is on the old and new state to decide whether anything changed. Mutating and passing back the same object means same reference, so React skips the render. The fix: `setUser({ ...user, name: 'Ada' })` — a new object, a new reference.
optionExplanations: Nested objects are fine in state; you just must replace rather than mutate them.
State can hold any value — objects, arrays, functions. The type isn't the issue.
Correct — same reference means React concludes nothing changed. Spread into a new object.
Batching delays renders by microseconds within an event, not until refresh. A refresh actually loses the state entirely.
variants.interviewTip: The phrase to use: 'React state updates rely on referential equality, so immutable updates are mandatory.' Interviewers listen for 'referential equality'.

variants.question: A shopping cart keeps `cart` in state. The remove handler runs `cart.splice(i, 1); setCart(cart);` and the deleted row stays on screen until an unrelated state change forces a render. What is the underlying cause?
options: Arrays past a certain length must switch from `useState` to `useReducer` to update
The render lagged only because React deliberately throttles all list state updates to 60fps
`splice` returns the removed elements, so `setCart` was handed the wrong value in this case
`splice` mutated the array in place, so `Object.is` sees the same reference and bails
variants.rationale: `splice` edits the array in place and returns the removed items, but the crux is the reference: `setCart` got the very same array object it already held, so `Object.is(prev, next)` is true and React bails out. The next unrelated update happens to re-render and reveal the already-mutated data. Fix with an immutable copy: `setCart(cart.filter((_, idx) => idx !== i))`.
optionExplanations: `useReducer` is an organizational choice, not a size requirement; `useState` handles arrays of any length fine.
There is no 60fps throttle causing this; the delayed appearance is a coincidental later render, not rate limiting.

While it's true `splice` returns the removed elements (not the new array), the code passes `cart` itself to `setCart`, not the return value — so the reason it fails is the unchanged reference, not a wrong value.
Correct — mutating in place keeps the same reference, and React's referential equality check concludes nothing changed.
variants.interviewTip: Name the trap explicitly: array methods like `splice`, `sort`, and `reverse` mutate in place. Say 'I reach for `filter`, `map`, or a spread to produce a new reference React can detect.'

variants.question: A leaderboard runs `setScores(scores.sort((a, b) => b.points - a.points))` when new results arrive, but the on-screen order never changes. A `console.log(scores)` right after confirms the array *is* sorted. What's going on?
options: `sort` runs asynchronously here, so `setScores` fired before the ordering had actually finished
`sort` orders in place and returns the same array, so `setScores` gets that reference and bails
Numeric comparators aren't supported here; React expects `localeCompare`-style comparators instead
The list is missing its `key` prop, so React simply can't detect that the ordering has now changed
variants.rationale: `Array.prototype.sort` mutates in place and returns the array it was called on. The log proves the data changed, but `Object.is(prev, next)` compares references, sees the same array, and React skips the render — the sorted data is invisible until some other update happens to re-render. Fix: `setScores([...scores].sort(...))` or the non-mutating `scores.toSorted(...)`.
optionExplanations: `sort` is fully synchronous; by the time `setScores` is called the array is already ordered — the log even proves it.
Correct — same array in, same reference out: React's referential equality check concludes nothing changed, so the already-sorted data never paints.
Numeric comparators are the standard JavaScript idiom and React never inspects them; the comparator isn't involved in the bailout.
Keys govern how list items are matched *during* a render; here no render happens at all, so keys never enter the picture.
variants.interviewTip: The devious part of this trap is that logging shows 'correct' data, which sends people hunting in the wrong place. Say: 'the state changed but the reference didn't — React answers to `Object.is`, not to `console.log`.'

variants.question: Hoping to 'avoid stale state', a developer writes `setForm(prev => { prev.email = value; return prev; })`. Now the email input stops updating entirely as the user types. Why doesn't the functional updater save them here?
options: It mutates `prev` and returns it, so `Object.is` is true and React skips the render
Functional updaters accept only primitive state values, never object state like this
React deep-freezes state objects, so assigning to `prev.email` throws an error silently
React defers functional updates a tick, so the value lands one keystroke behind the input
variants.rationale: The functional updater solves *staleness* (reading the latest state), not *immutability*. Whatever the updater returns is still compared to the previous state with `Object.is` — returning the mutated `prev` means same reference, so React bails out on every keystroke. The fix is to return a new object: `setForm(prev => ({ ...prev, email: value }))`.
optionExplanations: Correct — the updater's return value goes through the same referential equality check as any other update; mutating and returning `prev` guarantees a bailout.
Functional updaters work with any state shape — objects, arrays, Maps; the constraint is on references, not types.
React does not freeze your state objects; the assignment succeeds, which is exactly why the mutation is dangerous rather than loud.
Batching happens within the same event tick, not across keystrokes; here the update never lands at all because the reference never changed.
variants.interviewTip: Draw the distinction sharply: 'the functional updater fixes stale closures; spreading into a new object fixes referential equality. You often need both — `setForm(prev => ({ ...prev, email: value }))`.'

sections.heading: The rules of hooks and useEffect
paragraphs: Hooks must be called unconditionally at the top level of a component, in the same order every render — React tracks them by call order, not by name. A hook inside an `if` breaks that bookkeeping.

`useEffect(fn, deps)` runs `fn` after render, and again whenever a value in `deps` changes. Return a cleanup function and React runs it before the next effect and on unmount — that's where you clear intervals, abort fetches, and unsubscribe.

In development, `<StrictMode>` deliberately mounts, unmounts, and remounts each component, so effects run twice. That's not a bug to suppress — it's a stress test that exposes effects missing proper cleanup.
sections.summary: Always call hooks at the top level in a fixed order, and give every effect a cleanup function to undo whatever it started — subscriptions, timers, and in-flight requests all need an off-switch.

variants.question: In development, a `useEffect` that starts a `setInterval` fires twice and the intervals stack up. What's the correct response?
options: Return a cleanup that clears the interval; StrictMode is exposing missing cleanup
Move the `setInterval` call out of the component and into module scope instead of here
Remove StrictMode entirely, since the double-invocation is really just a React bug here
Wrap the effect in a `useRef` flag so that it can only ever run a single time
variants.rationale: StrictMode's mount-unmount-remount cycle simulates what genuinely happens in real apps (navigation, remounts). If the effect cleaned up after itself — `return () => clearInterval(id)` — the double-run would be harmless. The double-invoke found a real leak.
optionExplanations: Correct — cleanup makes effects remount-safe, which is exactly what StrictMode is verifying.
Module scope runs once per page load, can't access props/state correctly, and never cleans up — strictly worse.
Deleting the smoke detector doesn't put out the fire. In production, remounts happen naturally and the leak remains.
A run-once flag defeats the purpose: on a real unmount/remount your effect now never re-runs, leaving stale subscriptions.
variants.interviewTip: 'Why does my effect run twice?' is a deliberately planted interview trap. The winning answer names StrictMode, explains the remount simulation, and concludes: 'the fix is cleanup, not suppression.'

variants.question: A component subscribes to a WebSocket inside `useEffect(() => { socket.on('msg', handle) }, [])`. In development, every message now triggers `handle` twice, and users report duplicate chat lines. A teammate proposes adding a module-level `let subscribed = false` guard so the subscription is registered only once. Evaluate this.
options: The guard is right — a module-level boolean is the standard way to make effects idempotent
The fix is returning `() => socket.off('msg', handle)`; the remount reveals the leak
Move the subscription into `useLayoutEffect`, which StrictMode never double-invokes at all
Add `handle` to the dependency array so the effect resubscribes cleanly on every change
variants.rationale: The duplicate handler is a missing-cleanup leak that StrictMode's mount-unmount-remount surfaced. Returning `() => socket.off('msg', handle)` unsubscribes before the next mount, so exactly one live listener remains. A module-level flag would silence dev noise but leaves the listener dangling on real remounts (route changes), reintroducing duplicates in production.
optionExplanations: A module-level flag is shared across all instances and never resets on a genuine remount, so it hides the symptom while preserving the leak — the opposite of idempotent.
Correct — pairing each subscription with a matching unsubscribe in cleanup is what makes the effect remount-safe, which is what StrictMode checks.
`useLayoutEffect` is also double-invoked under StrictMode and is for synchronous DOM measurement, not for dodging cleanup; this doesn't address the leak.
Adding `handle` to deps causes more resubscribes, not fewer, and still leaks without a cleanup to remove the prior listener.
variants.interviewTip: Whenever you 'subscribe', 'listen', 'open', or 'start' something in an effect, immediately ask 'where do I unsubscribe?' The cleanup function is the answer, and it's what makes StrictMode's double-invoke a non-event.

variants.question: A profile page fetches with `useEffect(() => { fetch('/api/user/' + id).then(r => r.json()).then(setUser) }, [id])`. When the user clicks quickly from profile 1 to profile 2, the page sometimes settles on user 1's data even though `id` is 2. What is the disciplined fix?
options: Add `user` to the deps so the effect keeps re-running until the data matches the current id value
Switch to `useLayoutEffect` so that the fetch fully resolves before the browser has painted
In cleanup, abort via `AbortController` or an `ignore` flag so a stale response won't commit
Wrap `setUser` in `useCallback` so only the newest reference is allowed to update the state
variants.rationale: This is a race: the effect for `id=1` and the effect for `id=2` both have in-flight requests, and whichever resolves *last* wins. The cleanup function is the built-in place to invalidate the previous run — abort the fetch or set a closure-scoped `ignore = true` that the `.then` checks before calling `setUser`. This is also precisely the class of bug StrictMode's mount-unmount-remount is designed to flush out in development.
optionExplanations: Depending on `user` makes the effect re-run after its own `setUser`, inviting an infinite fetch loop while doing nothing to stop the stale response from landing first.
`useLayoutEffect` changes *when* the effect runs, not the ordering of network responses; the race between two in-flight requests is untouched.
Correct — each effect run must be able to cancel or disown its async work in cleanup, so only the newest run's response can ever reach state.
`setUser` from `useState` is already referentially stable across renders; wrapping it in `useCallback` is a no-op against a network race.
variants.interviewTip: Say the word 'race condition' out loud, then: 'every async effect needs a way to disown its result in cleanup — `AbortController` or an `ignore` flag.' Bonus points for noting StrictMode's double-invoke exists to surface exactly this.

variants.question: A component calls `useState('')` inside `if (props.editable) { ... }`. Everything works until `editable` flips mid-session, then React throws `Rendered more hooks than during the previous render`. What rule was broken, and why does React enforce it?
options: Hooks may not read props during render, so `editable` must be pulled from context instead
`useState` may run only once per component, and the conditional added a second colliding call
The error is just a StrictMode development artifact and won't ever occur in production builds
Hooks must run in the same order every render, since React tracks each by call position
variants.rationale: React keeps each component's hook state in an ordered list and pairs the Nth hook call of this render with the Nth slot from the last render. A hook inside `if` changes the count and order when the condition flips, so every hook after it reads the wrong slot — hence the hard error. The fix: call the hook unconditionally at the top level and branch inside the render logic (or inside the hook's usage) instead.
optionExplanations: Reading props during render is the entire point of components; the restriction is on *where* hooks are called, not what they read.
Components routinely call `useState` many times; the problem is the conditional call order, not the call count in itself.
This is a genuine invariant violation, not a StrictMode simulation — production crashes identically once the condition flips.
Correct — hooks are tracked by call order, so conditional calls shift every subsequent hook into the wrong state slot; that's why the rule exists.
variants.interviewTip: Don't just recite 'top level only' — explain the mechanism: 'React has no hook names, only call positions, so a skipped hook misaligns every hook after it.' Explaining *why* the rule exists is what separates senior answers.

sections.heading: Reconciliation and the key prop
paragraphs: When state changes, React re-runs the component and diffs the new element tree against the old one — reconciliation. For lists, React needs to know which rendered item corresponds to which data item across renders. That's the `key`.

Using the array index as a key works only for lists that never reorder, insert, or delete. If you delete item 0 from an index-keyed list, every remaining item shifts to a new key — React matches old item 1 to new key 0, and any DOM state (checkbox checks, input text, focus) attaches to the wrong rows.
A key should be a stable identity from the data itself — a database id — so a reordered item keeps its component instance and its state.
sections.summary: Give each list item a stable `key` from your data, like an id, so its state follows it when the list changes. Keys must be unique among siblings and stable across renders — never the array index for a list that reorders, and never a value minted during render.

variants.question: A todo list uses `key={index}`. Each row has an uncontrolled checkbox. When the user deletes the first todo, the remaining rows' checkboxes appear shifted onto the wrong items. What happened?
options: The delete handler mutated the array in place, corrupting the underlying list order
The browser dropped the checkbox state at some point during the repaint after the deletion
Index keys identify rows by position, so DOM state stays put as the data shifts under it
Uncontrolled inputs simply can't be rendered inside mapped lists in React under any conditions
variants.rationale: With index keys, 'row 0' is a stable identity even though its data changed. React reuses the row-0 DOM (with its checked checkbox) for what is now a different todo. Stable ids as keys make identity follow the data instead of the position.
optionExplanations: Even a perfectly immutable delete produces this bug if keys are indexes — the keys, not the mutation, are at fault.
The browser preserved state perfectly — at each position. That's precisely the problem: position kept the state, data moved.
Correct — this is the canonical `key={index}` failure, and a top-tier interview trap.
Uncontrolled inputs in lists are fine when keys are stable identities.
variants.interviewTip: Don't just say 'index keys are bad'. Demonstrate the failure: 'delete the first row and every checkbox shifts up one item.' Concrete symptoms beat rules.

variants.question: A sortable table renders rows with `key={index}`. Each row has a `<input>` where the user is mid-typing an edit. When another user's update arrives and the list re-sorts so the focused row moves from position 3 to position 0, the half-typed text suddenly appears in a completely different row. Which statement best explains and fixes this?
options: Uncontrolled inputs can't coexist with sorting, so a controlled `value` prop is the only real fix
The sort mutated the array, so React rebuilt every row and reassigned the typed text at random
React re-sorts the DOM but never moves focus, so the typed text lags a single frame behind it
Index keys bind input state to a slot, so position 0 keeps old text; a stable row id fixes it
variants.rationale: With `key={index}`, key `0` always means 'whatever sits in position 0'. After the re-sort, React matches the old position-0 instance (holding the in-progress input value and focus) to the new position-0 data — a different record. Keying by a stable `row.id` makes React move the instance along with its data, so the input follows the row it belongs to.
optionExplanations: Controlled inputs don't fix keying: if the controlled value is looked up by index too, it desyncs the same way; the key is the root cause.
Even an immutable, freshly-sorted array reproduces this with index keys; the mutation is a red herring.
This isn't a one-frame focus lag; the input state is durably attached to the wrong record because identity is positional.
Correct — positional keys keep DOM/input state at each slot while the underlying data reorders, the classic reorder failure; stable ids fix it.
variants.interviewTip: Push past deletion examples — reordering is the harder case. Say 'with index keys, the key describes a slot, not a record, so any reorder detaches state from data.'

variants.question: A chat log renders newest-first and *prepends* each incoming message, using `key={index}`. Two symptoms appear: the Profiler shows every existing row re-rendering on each new message, and a row's open emoji picker jumps to a neighboring message. What explains both?
options: Prepending re-indexes every row, so nothing is stable: content changes defeat bailout and picker state stalls
Prepending to an array is O(n), and that one expensive copy is what drives both the re-renders and the glitch here
React can't diff lists rendered newest-first; storing them oldest-first and reversing them in CSS fixes both here
Popovers can't live inside keyed lists without a portal, and that one missing portal also forces the extra renders
variants.rationale: With index keys, a prepend re-labels every message: the item that was key `0` is now key `1`, and so on. React matches by key, so it pairs each old row with a *different* message's data — every row's props 'changed' (mass re-render) and any state held per row (the open picker) stays with its position while the message it belonged to moves down. Keying by the message id makes only the one new row mount and keeps state glued to its message.
optionExplanations: Correct — prepending is the stress test that breaks index keys in both directions at once: no stable keys means no render bailouts *and* positional state detaching from data.
Copying even a few thousand array elements is microseconds; the cost and the misattached picker both trace to key identity, not array mechanics.
React diffs any ordering fine; the direction of the list is irrelevant when keys carry stable identity.
Portals change where DOM is attached, not how reconciliation matches rows; keyed lists host popovers without issue when keys are stable.
variants.interviewTip: Deletion, reordering, *and prepending* all break index keys — prepending is the sneakiest because the list 'looks' append-only in the code. Say: 'any operation that changes an item's position rewrites its identity under index keys.'

variants.question: Having read that index keys are dangerous, a developer switches a list to `key={crypto.randomUUID()}`, generating the id during render. Now every keystroke in a row's `<input>` blurs the field, and row animations restart on every parent render. Why?
options: Random UUIDs collide now and then, and the duplicate keys corrupt React's internal diffing structures
A key made during render differs every pass, so React remounts each row, destroying focus and state
Keys have to be stable-length strings, and this variable randomness breaks the reconciler's hashing
The blur comes from the inputs being uncontrolled; random keys are otherwise a fine fix for index keys
variants.rationale: A key is an identity claim. Generating it during render tells React 'this is a row it has never seen' on every single pass, so reconciliation can never match old to new: every row is torn down and rebuilt, taking focus, input contents, scroll, and animation state with it. This is strictly worse than index keys. The id must be created *once* — when the data is created — and stored on the record, not minted in render.
optionExplanations: UUID collisions are vanishingly rare and not the mechanism here; the keys fail because they are *always* different, not occasionally identical.
Correct — a changed key means a new identity, and a new identity means unmount-and-remount; render-time key generation guarantees that on every render.
React compares keys with simple equality; their length and format are irrelevant to reconciliation.
Controlled inputs would preserve the *value* but still lose focus and remount the DOM node each render; the key strategy is the root cause.
variants.interviewTip: Frame the spectrum: 'index keys give unstable identity on reorder; random keys give no identity at all. The requirement is a key that is unique among siblings *and* stable across renders — which is why it belongs in the data.'

sections.heading: Lifting state and the single source of truth
paragraphs: When two components need the same data, move that state to their closest common ancestor and pass it down as props — 'lifting state up'. The alternative, copying the data into both, creates two sources of truth that drift apart.

The same principle covers derived data: if it can be computed from existing state (`filteredItems` from `items` + `query`), compute it during render. Storing derived data in its own `useState` means remembering to update two things forever.

Reach for context only when props would have to tunnel through many indifferent layers (prop drilling), and for effects only to synchronize with systems *outside* React — never to 'react' to your own state.
sections.summary: Keep shared data in one place and pass it down, and if a value can be calculated from what you have, just calculate it.

variants.question: A component stores `items` in state, and also stores `filteredItems` in a second useState, updated via a useEffect whenever `items` or `query` changes. What's the idiomatic improvement?
options: Compute filteredItems in render (maybe useMemo) and drop the second state
Move filteredItems into a global store so the two copies can't desync anymore
Debounce the syncing effect so the two states fall out of step less often
Add filteredItems to the effect's dependency array so it stays in sync too
variants.rationale: Derived data shouldn't be state. `const filteredItems = items.filter(...)` during render is always consistent by construction — there's nothing to sync, no extra render pass, no effect. useMemo is an optional optimization if the filter is genuinely expensive.
optionExplanations: Correct — 'you might not need an effect': derive it, don't store it.
A global store still duplicates the truth; you've just moved the desync risk somewhere with more ceremony.
Debouncing makes the stale window longer, not the design better.
Adding the derived value to the deps risks an infinite loop (effect sets state, state re-triggers effect) and deepens the anti-pattern.
variants.interviewTip: The React docs page 'You Might Not Need an Effect' is quietly one of the most quoted sources in React interviews. 'Derived state should be computed, not stored' is the sentence to say.

variants.question: A checkout page keeps `lineItems` in state. It also keeps `total` in a separate `useState`, recomputed inside a `useEffect` that watches `lineItems`. QA reports the total occasionally lags a render behind the items — for one paint it shows the previous total. What's the correct redesign?
options: Wrap the `setTotal` call in `flushSync` so that the total commits synchronously alongside the items
Compute `total` in render via `lineItems.reduce(...)` and delete the `total` state and its effect
Move the total computation into a `useLayoutEffect` so it always runs before the browser paints
Store the total in a `useRef` and mutate that ref directly whenever `lineItems` happens to change
variants.rationale: The one-frame lag is inherent to storing derived data in state: the component renders with new `lineItems` and the old `total`, then the effect fires and triggers a second render with the corrected total. Computing `total` inline during render makes it consistent with `lineItems` on the very first paint — no effect, no extra render, no stale window.
optionExplanations: `flushSync` forces a synchronous commit but keeps the redundant second render and the anti-pattern; it patches timing instead of removing the duplicated source of truth.
Correct — the total is derivable, so compute it in render; there's nothing to sync and no lag by construction.
`useLayoutEffect` narrows the visible lag but still stores derived data and adds an extra pass; it treats the symptom, not the cause.
A ref holds a value across renders but doesn't trigger re-render, so the displayed total would go stale — worse, not better.
variants.interviewTip: The tell for this anti-pattern is 'a value that's always recomputed from other state inside an effect.' Answer: 'if it's derivable, derive it in render — effects that mirror state into more state cause exactly this off-by-one-render lag.'

variants.question: A `ProductList` and a `ProductDetail` sit side by side. Each keeps its own `selectedId` in `useState`, and each calls a callback to push changes into the other's state. Occasionally a rapid double-click leaves the list highlighting one product while the detail pane shows another. What's the principled fix?
options: Add a parent `useEffect` that watches both values and reconciles them whenever they disagree
Share `selectedId` through a ref in context so the updates bypass re-render timing entirely here
Have `ProductDetail` read the list's state via a forwarded ref, making the list the true owner
Lift `selectedId` to the common ancestor and pass it down, so disagreement can't be represented
variants.rationale: Two copies of the same fact, synced by hand, will eventually drift — the double-click just exposes the window between the two setters. Lifting the state up replaces synchronization with sharing: the ancestor owns `selectedId`, both children render from the same value, and there is no second copy to fall out of step. This is the canonical 'lifting state up' refactor.
optionExplanations: A reconciling effect is a third participant in the sync dance — it fires a render *after* the disagreement has already painted, and choosing which copy 'wins' is itself a bug farm.
A ref doesn't trigger re-renders, so components reading it would display stale selections; it trades a drift bug for a staleness bug.
Reaching into a sibling's internals through refs inverts the data-flow model and still leaves two stateful owners; props-down is the supported direction.
Correct — duplicated state is the disease and syncing is a symptom-patch; a single lifted owner makes the two panes consistent by construction.
variants.interviewTip: The phrase 'single source of truth' lands best with the follow-up: 'I don't sync state, I share it — if two components can disagree, the state is owned in the wrong place.'

variants.question: A signup form keeps `email` and `password` in state, plus a third state `isValid`, updated by a `useEffect` watching both fields. The submit button enables one keystroke late, so a teammate proposes *also* calling `setIsValid` inside each `onChange` handler. Evaluate the proposal.
options: Sound — writing `isValid` at the event source kills the lag, and the effect stays on as a safety net
Close, but the effect should become a `useLayoutEffect` so validity corrects before the browser paints
Wrong way — drop the `isValid` state and effect and compute `validate(email, password)` in render
Wrong way — merge all three values into one `useReducer` so field and validity updates commit atomically
variants.rationale: `isValid` is a pure function of `email` and `password`, so storing it means the component can render with fresh fields and a stale flag — that *is* the one-keystroke lag. The teammate's patch adds a third write site to keep in sync, deepening the anti-pattern. Deriving the value in render makes it correct on the same pass the fields change, with less code and no effect at all.
optionExplanations: Duplicating the write into every handler means validity logic now lives in N places; miss one handler (paste, autofill) and the drift returns.
`useLayoutEffect` hides the visible flash but keeps the redundant state, the extra render pass, and the synchronization burden.
Correct — a derivable value should never be state; computing it in render eliminates the lag and the entire category of desync bugs.
A reducer centralizes updates but each action must still remember to recompute `isValid` — the second source of truth survives, just relocated.
variants.interviewTip: When offered a fix, first ask whether the state should exist at all. 'Can this be computed from what I already have?' — if yes, say 'delete the state, derive in render' before discussing anything about timing.

sections.heading: Render performance: memo, useMemo, useCallback
paragraphs: By default, when a component re-renders, all of its children re-render too — regardless of whether their props changed. Usually that's fine; renders are cheap. Optimize when profiling says so, not before.

`React.memo(Child)` skips re-rendering Child if its props are shallowly equal to last time. But props created inline — `onClick={() => ...}`, `style={{...}}` — are new objects every render, so they defeat memo. `useCallback` and `useMemo` stabilize those references.
This trio is a package deal: memo on the child does nothing useful if the parent passes a fresh callback each render, and useCallback without a memoized child mostly adds overhead.
sections.summary: Don't optimize until profiling shows you need to, and when you do, keep prop references stable — with `useCallback` for functions and `useMemo` for objects/arrays — so `memo` can actually skip renders.

variants.question: A parent renders `<ExpensiveChild onSave={() => save(id)} />` where ExpensiveChild is wrapped in React.memo, yet it still re-renders every time the parent does. Why?
options: `onSave` is a reserved prop name that quietly bypasses memoization altogether here
React.memo only ever applies to class components, and never once to function components
The inline arrow is a fresh reference each render, so memo's shallow compare sees change
memo compares its props deeply, and the save function's body changed between the renders
variants.rationale: memo does a shallow (reference) comparison. A fresh arrow function is a fresh reference every render, so `onSave` never compares equal. Wrap it: `const onSave = useCallback(() => save(id), [id])` — now the reference is stable and memo can bail out.
optionExplanations: There are no reserved prop names that bypass memo; the mechanism is purely reference equality.
React.memo is specifically for function components (classes have PureComponent).
Correct — inline functions and object literals are the classic memo-defeaters.
memo is shallow by default; it never inspects function bodies, only references.
variants.interviewTip: Great senior-signal answer: 'memo, useMemo, and useCallback are one system — stable references in, skipped renders out. And I only reach for them after the Profiler shows a problem.'

variants.question: A developer wraps `<Chart data={rows.filter(r => r.active)} />` in `React.memo` and also passes `config={{ theme: 'dark' }}` inline. They've already stabilized every callback with `useCallback`, yet Chart still re-renders on every parent render. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
options: React.memo compares only primitive props, so any object or array prop disables it completely
The filter runs on every render, and that call mutates `rows` and invalidates memo's cache
`useCallback` doesn't stabilize the component itself, so callbacks recreate and still break memo
The `data` array and `config` object are built fresh inline each render; they need `useMemo`
variants.rationale: `useCallback` fixes function props, but here the memo-defeaters are a freshly-filtered array (`rows.filter(...)`) and an inline object literal (`{ theme: 'dark' }`) — each is a new reference every render. memo's shallow compare sees changed props and re-renders. Fix: `const data = useMemo(() => rows.filter(r => r.active), [rows])` and hoist the constant config out of the component (or `useMemo` it).
optionExplanations: memo compares object/array props fine by reference; stable references (via `useMemo`) allow it to bail out — objects don't disable it.
`filter` returns a new array without mutating `rows`; the fresh reference, not mutation, is what defeats memo.
The callbacks are already stabilized with `useCallback`, so they aren't the problem; the array and object props are.
Correct — inline array/object literals are new references each render and defeat memo's shallow comparison just like inline functions do.
variants.interviewTip: Interviewers escalate from callbacks to values. The complete answer: 'stabilize every non-primitive prop — functions with `useCallback`, arrays/objects with `useMemo` or hoisting — or memo can never bail out.'

variants.question: `Sidebar` is wrapped in `React.memo` and receives one stable primitive prop plus JSX children: `<Sidebar width={W}><nav>{links}</nav></Sidebar>`. Every callback in the app is already memoized, yet the Profiler shows `Sidebar` re-rendering whenever its parent does. What's the diagnosis?
options: `React.memo` deliberately ignores the `children` prop, so something else entirely must cause the re-render
JSX children are a fresh element each render and `children` is a prop, so shallow compare changes
`width` being a primitive forces re-renders, since memo can only ever bail out when all props are objects
memo compares the element trees deeply, and the `<nav>` subtree is too large, so it re-renders defensively
variants.rationale: `<nav>{links}</nav>` is a call that returns a new element object each time the parent renders, and that object is passed as the `children` prop. To memo's shallow compare, `children !== prevChildren` every single time, so the bailout never fires. Fixes: hoist truly static children to a constant outside the component, wrap the element in `useMemo`, or restructure so the parent passes children it received (which stay referentially stable when the parent re-renders for its own state).
optionExplanations: `children` participates in the shallow comparison exactly like named props — memo doesn't special-case it, which is precisely why inline JSX defeats it.
Correct — inline JSX is an object literal in disguise; the freshly created element makes the `children` prop fail reference equality on every render.
Primitives are memo's easiest case: compared by value, `width={W}` matches whenever `W` is unchanged. It's not the culprit.
memo never walks element trees; the comparison is shallow and reference-based, and there is no size-based defensive re-render.
variants.interviewTip: Few candidates realize JSX children are just another prop holding a freshly allocated element. Saying '`children` fails shallow comparison because JSX creates a new element object per render' is a genuine differentiator.

variants.question: Every consumer of `ThemeContext` is wrapped in `React.memo`, yet all of them re-render whenever `App` re-renders for unrelated reasons. The provider reads `<ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, setTheme }}>`. Why doesn't memo help, and what's the fix?
options: The inline `value` is new each render, so context notifies all consumers and memo can't block it; memoize it
`setTheme` gets a fresh identity each render, so wrapping it in `useCallback` alone stabilizes the value object
Consumers must be wrapped in `useMemo` on top of `React.memo` before they are able to skip context updates
A provider re-render always re-renders every consumer regardless of value; splitting into contexts is the only fix
variants.rationale: Context propagation runs on its own track: a consumer re-renders whenever the provider's `value` fails `Object.is` against the previous one, and `React.memo` (which guards *props*) has no say in it. An object literal in the provider's JSX fails that check on every render, so every consumer wakes up even when `theme` is unchanged. Memoizing the value object with `useMemo` restores a stable reference between actual theme changes.
optionExplanations: Correct — context updates bypass memo entirely, so the only lever is the `value` reference itself; a memoized object makes unrelated parent renders invisible to consumers.
The `setTheme` returned by `useState` is already stable across renders — the fresh *wrapper object* is the culprit, and `useCallback` on a stable function changes nothing.
`useMemo` memoizes computed values inside a component; it isn't a component wrapper and has no role in whether a consumer responds to context.

Consumers re-render on value *change* (`Object.is`), not on every provider render — with a memoized value they correctly skip. Context splitting is a real optimization for unrelated values, but it's not the only or primary fix here.
variants.interviewTip: State the exception crisply: '`React.memo` guards props, not context — a context consumer re-renders whenever the provider value fails `Object.is`, so provider values must be memoized like any other non-primitive.'

sections.heading: useContext and prop drilling
paragraphs: Context lets a value skip the prop chain: a `<Provider value={x}>` high in the tree, and any descendant reads it with `useContext(TheContext)` without every layer in between forwarding a prop it doesn't care about. That's the cure for prop drilling — threading `user` or `theme` through ten components just so the eleventh can use it.

Context is a delivery mechanism, not a state manager. It doesn't store or update anything on its own; you still hold the state with `useState` or `useReducer` at the provider and put the value on the provider. A common, clean pattern is to pair a state context with a dispatch context so components that only trigger changes don't re-render when the data changes.

The cost to respect: every consumer re-renders when the provider `value` changes by `Object.is`, and `React.memo` can't stop it. So don't reach for context for values that change every keystroke, memoize the `value` object, and split unrelated concerns into separate contexts rather than bundling them into one.
sections.summary: Context delivers a value straight to deep consumers so you skip prop drilling, but it's a pipe, not a store — keep the state elsewhere and memoize the provider value.

variants.question: A `theme` prop is forwarded through six intermediate components that never use it, just to reach a deep `Button`. What's the idiomatic fix?
options: Store the theme on a `window` global so that any component anywhere can read it without passing props
Put `theme` in context and read it in `Button` with `useContext`, skipping the middle layers
Duplicate the theme into each component's own state so nothing has to be forwarded at all
Merge the six components into one so there's no chain left for the prop to travel through
variants.rationale: Threading a prop through components that don't use it is textbook prop drilling. Context solves exactly this: a provider near the top and a `useContext` read in `Button`, with the six middle layers left untouched. They no longer need to know the theme exists.
optionExplanations: A `window` global sits outside React, so changing it won't trigger re-renders and you lose SSR safety and testability.
Correct — context delivers the value directly to the consumer, so the indifferent middle layers stop forwarding a prop they never read.
Copying the theme into six states creates six sources of truth that drift; the whole point is one shared value.
Collapsing components to dodge drilling destroys your composition; context removes the drilling without flattening the tree.
variants.interviewTip: Name the smell first: 'this is prop drilling.' Then prescribe: 'context, or component composition — passing the element as `children` — depending on how deep and how dynamic the value is.'

variants.question: A `SettingsProvider` holds `<Provider value={{ settings, updateSettings }}>` with the object literal inline. Consumers wrapped in `React.memo` still re-render on every unrelated `App` render. What's the fix?
options: Memoize the provider's `value` object so its reference is stable between real changes
Wrap every consumer in a second `React.memo`, which finally lets them ignore the context
Move `settings` onto a `useRef` inside the provider so writing to it never causes a re-render
Replace `useContext` with a custom hook, since `useContext` subscribes far too eagerly by design
variants.rationale: The inline `{ settings, updateSettings }` is a new object every render, so the provider's `value` fails `Object.is` on every `App` render and notifies all consumers — a check `React.memo` has no power over. Wrapping the object in `useMemo(() => ({ settings, updateSettings }), [settings])` gives it a stable reference, so consumers only wake up when `settings` actually changes.
optionExplanations: Correct — a memoized `value` object keeps its reference between genuine changes, so unrelated parent renders no longer trip the context's `Object.is` check.
`React.memo` guards props, not context subscriptions; stacking more of it does nothing to stop a changed provider value.
A ref doesn't trigger re-renders at all, so consumers would read stale settings — it trades the re-render bug for a staleness bug.
A custom hook wrapping `useContext` reads the same context identically; the subscription behavior is unchanged, so the object churn remains.
variants.interviewTip: Say it as a rule: 'inline provider values re-render every consumer — memoize the value, and split dispatch from data so setters-only consumers don't wake for data changes.'

variants.question: A component calls `useContext(AuthContext)` but always reads `null` instead of the logged-in user. The provider clearly wraps the page. What's the most likely cause?
options: `useContext` can only be called from the same file where `createContext` was originally declared
The component sits above the provider in the tree, so it falls back to the default value
Context values are asynchronous, so the first read is always `null` until a later effect resolves
Two React copies are bundled, so the context instance the reader sees differs from the one provided
variants.rationale: `useContext` reads from the nearest matching provider *above* the calling component. If the reader is rendered outside (above, or in a sibling branch of) the provider, there's no provider on its path and it gets the default passed to `createContext` — often `null`. Move the provider up so it wraps the reader, or move the reader inside it.
optionExplanations: You can call `useContext` anywhere the context object is imported; file location is irrelevant to how it resolves.
Correct — context resolves to the nearest provider above the reader, so a reader outside the provider's subtree falls back to the default value.
Context reads are synchronous and return the current value immediately; there's no async first-null behavior.
Duplicate-React bundling can break context, but it's a rare tooling edge case, not the likely cause when a single app simply nests the reader wrong.
variants.interviewTip: Debug it out loud: 'the reader must be a descendant of the provider — I'd check the tree position first, then confirm the default I passed to `createContext` explains the value I'm seeing.'

variants.question: A team puts *all* app state — user, theme, cart, notifications — into one giant context. The app feels sluggish; typing in a search box re-renders the whole tree. What's the core problem?
options: One context per app is a hard React limit, so bundling state is the only supported approach here
Context is inherently slow, so any nontrivial app must adopt an external store like Redux instead
Every consumer re-renders when any field changes, since they all share one `value` reference
The context wasn't wrapped in `React.memo`, which would have let unaffected consumers skip renders
variants.rationale: Context notifies every consumer whenever the provider `value` changes by reference. Bundling unrelated state into one object means a search-box keystroke changes that object, so components that only read `theme` or `cart` re-render too. Split into focused contexts (or separate state/dispatch contexts) so a change touches only the consumers that read that slice.
optionExplanations: You can create as many contexts as you like; splitting them is the standard fix, not a workaround for a limit.
Context isn't inherently slow — it's fine when scoped; the sluggishness comes from bundling unrelated state, and an external store isn't required.
Correct — a single shared `value` means any field's change re-renders all consumers, so unrelated state must be split into separate contexts.
`React.memo` can't intercept context updates at all; the fix is narrower contexts, not memoizing consumers.
variants.interviewTip: Show you know the granularity trade-off: 'context has no selector, so a consumer subscribes to the whole value — I split by concern, or reach for a store with selectors when slices get fine-grained.'

sections.heading: useRef and reaching the DOM
paragraphs: `useRef` gives you a mutable box — `{ current: ... }` — that persists across renders and, crucially, does *not* trigger a re-render when you change `.current`. That makes it the right tool for two distinct jobs: getting a handle to a DOM node (`<input ref={inputRef}>`, then `inputRef.current.focus()`), and stashing a mutable value that shouldn't drive the UI, like an interval id or the latest value for a callback.

The dividing line against state is visibility: if changing a value should update what the user sees, it's state; if it's bookkeeping the render doesn't depend on, it's a ref. Writing to a ref during render is a code smell (renders should be pure); read and write refs in effects and event handlers instead, where side effects belong.

A DOM ref is only populated *after* the DOM is committed, so `ref.current` is `null` during the first render and available by the time effects run. To expose a ref to a parent through a custom component, pass it as an ordinary prop (React 19) or use `forwardRef` (earlier versions).
sections.summary: Use a ref for a value that persists across renders without causing one — a DOM node handle or mutable bookkeeping — and read it in effects or handlers, never as a substitute for state the UI depends on.

variants.question: You need to move keyboard focus to an `<input>` right after the component mounts. What's the standard approach?
options: Query the input with `document.getElementById` inside the component's render function
Attach a `ref` to the input and call `ref.current.focus()` inside a mount effect
Store the input's value in state and re-render until the browser gives it focus on its own
Set the HTML `autofocus` attribute and trust it to fire reliably across every route change
variants.rationale: A ref is React's supported handle to a DOM node. Attach `ref={inputRef}` to the input, then in a `useEffect(() => inputRef.current?.focus(), [])` — which runs after the DOM is committed — call `.focus()`. The ref is guaranteed populated by the time the effect runs.
optionExplanations: Reaching into the DOM with `getElementById` during render bypasses React's model and runs before the node may even exist.
Correct — a ref gives you the committed DOM node, and a mount effect is the right moment to imperatively focus it.
State drives rendering, not focus; no amount of re-rendering will move the caret into an input.
The `autofocus` attribute is unreliable across client-side navigation and doesn't re-fire when a component remounts on the same page.
variants.interviewTip: Frame it as 'imperative escape hatch': 'React is declarative, but focus, scroll, media playback, and measurement are imperative — I reach for a ref and do it in an effect.'

variants.question: A developer stores a running counter in `useRef(0)`, increments `ref.current++` in the click handler, and renders `{ref.current}`. The number on screen never updates until something else re-renders. Why?
options: Mutating a ref's `.current` doesn't schedule a re-render, so the UI won't reflect the new value
Refs hold only DOM nodes, so storing a number in one silently coerces it back to `null`
The increment ran during render, and React discards any ref writes that happen mid-render
The `ref` needs to be listed in some dependency array before React will ever show its current value
variants.rationale: Refs are deliberately render-invisible: writing `.current` is a side effect that doesn't tell React anything changed, so the component doesn't re-render and the displayed number goes stale. A counter the UI displays is state, not a ref — use `useState` so each increment schedules a render.
optionExplanations: Correct — a ref write doesn't schedule a render, so a value the UI depends on belongs in state, not a ref.
Refs hold any value — numbers, objects, functions; there's no coercion to `null` for non-DOM values.
The write happened in a click handler, not during render; even so, React doesn't 'discard' ref writes — it just doesn't react to them.
Refs aren't reactive dependencies; listing one changes nothing, because ref changes don't participate in rendering at all.
variants.interviewTip: The one-liner: 'if the UI reads it, it's state; if it's bookkeeping the render ignores, it's a ref.' Displaying a ref's value is the classic misuse.

variants.question: A parent component wants to call a `focus()` method on a child input, but `<TextField ref={ref} />` gives `ref.current === null` even after mount. What's the missing piece (pre-React-19)?
options: `ref` is a reserved word on components, so the prop must be renamed to `inputRef` to pass through
Refs can only point at native DOM elements and never at a custom component, so this can't work
The child must forward the ref to a real DOM node, e.g. via `forwardRef`, to be reachable
The parent has to wrap the child in `React.memo` before a ref will attach to it correctly
variants.rationale: By default a `ref` on a custom component isn't forwarded to any DOM node — there's nothing for `.current` to point at, so it stays `null`. Wrapping the child in `forwardRef` (React 18 and earlier) and attaching the forwarded ref to its inner `<input>` connects the parent's ref to the real node; in React 19 `ref` is a normal prop and can be passed straight through.
optionExplanations: Renaming to `inputRef` is one manual workaround, but the actual mechanism the question wants is forwarding the ref to a DOM node.
Refs can absolutely point at custom components' internals — that's exactly what ref forwarding enables.
Correct — a custom component must forward the ref down to a real DOM node (via `forwardRef` pre-19) for the parent's ref to resolve.
`React.memo` controls re-render skipping and has nothing to do with whether a ref reaches a DOM node.
variants.interviewTip: Mention the version split: 'pre-19 I'd use `forwardRef`; in React 19 `ref` is just a prop. Either way I expose an imperative handle deliberately, not by default.'

variants.question: Inside render, a component writes `renderCountRef.current = someProp` and later an effect reads it. A reviewer flags the render-time write. Why is writing a ref during render discouraged?
options: Ref writes during render throw an exception in Strict Mode, so the whole component crashes hard on the second render pass
Renders must be pure; a render-time side effect breaks under bail-outs, StrictMode, and concurrent features
Refs are frozen until the commit phase, so any assignment during render is silently ignored anyway
Writing a ref in render permanently disables that ref's ability to hold a DOM node later on
variants.rationale: React treats rendering as a pure calculation it may run extra times, bail out of, or throw away (StrictMode double-invoke, concurrent rendering). A ref write is a mutation — a side effect — so doing it in render means the value depends on how many times React happened to render, which is unpredictable. Move the write into an effect or event handler, where side effects are expected.
optionExplanations: StrictMode double-invokes render to *expose* impurity, but it doesn't throw on a ref write; the problem is unpredictability, not a crash.
Correct — renders must be pure, and a render-time ref mutation is a side effect that misbehaves under double-invocation, bail-outs, and concurrent rendering.
Refs aren't frozen during render; the assignment does take effect, which is exactly why an accidental extra render corrupts it.
A ref that held a value can still receive a DOM node later; render-time writes don't disable that.
variants.interviewTip: Tie it to purity: 'render is a pure function React can call any number of times, so I keep side effects — including ref writes — out of it and inside effects or handlers.'

sections.heading: Controlled and uncontrolled forms
paragraphs: A controlled input hands its value to React: `value={x}` plus `onChange={e => setX(e.target.value)}`. React state is the single source of truth, the DOM only ever displays it, and you can validate, format, or disable on every keystroke. An uncontrolled input keeps its own value in the DOM; you read it when needed via a ref or on submit, and optionally seed it with `defaultValue`.

The classic bug is going halfway: passing `value` *without* an `onChange` makes a read-only field the user can't type into (React keeps resetting the DOM to the fixed state value). React warns about this. The fix is either to add the `onChange` (making it controlled) or to switch `value` to `defaultValue` (making it uncontrolled).

Reach for controlled when you need live interaction — instant validation, conditional formatting, or enabling submit as the user types. Reach for uncontrolled (or a form library) for simple forms where you only need values at submit time and want to avoid a re-render per keystroke. A single input should be one or the other for its whole life; switching between them mid-flight triggers a warning.
sections.summary: A controlled input mirrors React state with `value` + `onChange` and gives you per-keystroke control; an uncontrolled input owns its value in the DOM and you read it with a ref — pick one per field and don't pass `value` without `onChange`.

variants.question: A developer renders `<input value={name} />` with no `onChange`. The field displays the initial name but the user can't type into it. Why?
options: The input is disabled by default until an `onChange` handler is explicitly attached to it
`value` binds the field to state, so with no `onChange` React resets each keystroke away
React inputs need a `name` attribute before the browser will accept any typed keystrokes
Text inputs require a surrounding `<form>` element or they silently reject user typing
variants.rationale: Passing `value` makes the input controlled: React forces the DOM to match the state on every render. With no `onChange`, the state never updates, so each keystroke is immediately overwritten back to the fixed `name`. Add `onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)}`, or use `defaultValue` if you meant it to be uncontrolled.
optionExplanations: The input isn't disabled — it's controlled; React actively resets it, which looks like disabling but is a different mechanism.
Correct — a `value` prop with no `onChange` locks the field to unchanging state, so React reverts every keystroke.
A `name` attribute affects form submission, not whether typing registers; it isn't required to accept input.
Inputs work outside a `<form>` just fine; the wrapping element isn't why typing is rejected.
variants.interviewTip: This is a rite-of-passage React warning. Say: 'value without onChange is a read-only controlled input — either add the handler or switch to defaultValue.'

variants.question: A form needs to enable its Submit button only once both fields are non-empty, and highlight invalid fields as the user types. Controlled or uncontrolled, and why?
options: Controlled — React state per field lets you validate and toggle Submit on every keystroke
Uncontrolled — reading the fields via refs on submit keeps typing fast and avoids re-renders
Uncontrolled — the `required` attribute handles both the disabling and the highlighting for free
Either works identically, so the choice here is purely a matter of personal preference
variants.rationale: The requirement is live, per-keystroke behavior: re-validate and re-evaluate the Submit button as the user types. That's exactly what controlled inputs give you — the value lives in React state, so every change re-renders with the new validity. Uncontrolled inputs only surface their value on demand, so you'd have no natural moment to react keystroke-by-keystroke.
optionExplanations: Correct — controlled state re-renders on each keystroke, which is what live validation and a dynamically enabled Submit require.
Refs-on-submit reads values only when you ask, so there's no per-keystroke hook to drive live validation and button state.
`required` blocks native submission but doesn't give you live per-keystroke highlighting or a React-controlled disabled state.
They differ precisely on live interaction; the need to react on every keystroke makes controlled the fit here.
variants.interviewTip: Decide by interactivity: 'need live validation, formatting, or conditional UI as they type? Controlled. Just need values at submit? Uncontrolled is lighter.'

variants.question: A component renders `<input value={value} onChange={handle} />` but initializes `useState(props.initial)` which is sometimes `undefined`. The console warns about switching from uncontrolled to controlled. What's the cause?
options: React bans deriving any initial state value from incoming props, which triggers this exact warning
The input started with an `undefined` value (uncontrolled), then became a defined string (controlled)
`onChange` must be wrapped in `useCallback`, or React treats the input as uncontrolled by default
Mixing `value` and `defaultValue` on one single input is what actually produces this controlled/uncontrolled warning
variants.rationale: React decides controlled-ness from whether `value` is defined. When `props.initial` is `undefined`, `value={undefined}` on the first render means React sees no value and treats the input as uncontrolled; once the user types (or props arrive) and `value` becomes a string, it flips to controlled — hence the warning. Fix by defaulting: `useState(props.initial ?? '')`, so `value` is always a defined string.
optionExplanations: Initializing state from props is perfectly allowed; the warning is about the value going from undefined to defined, not about the prop source.
Correct — `value={undefined}` reads as uncontrolled, and later becoming a defined string flips it to controlled, which triggers the warning.
`useCallback` affects reference stability, not controlled-ness; the input is controlled as long as `value` is defined.
There's no `defaultValue` here — the single `value` prop transitioning from undefined to defined is the actual trigger.
variants.interviewTip: Prevent it at the source: 'I default controlled values to an empty string — `value={x ?? ""}` — so an input is controlled from its very first render and never flips.'

variants.question: A large form re-renders visibly on every keystroke because all 20 fields are controlled in one component's state. A teammate wants to keep live validation only on the email field. What's a reasonable approach?
options: Make every field uncontrolled and read all 20 values from refs on submit for maximum speed
Keep email controlled for live validation and let simpler fields be uncontrolled or locally isolated
Wrap the entire form component in `React.memo`, which reliably prevents the keystroke re-renders across all fields
Move all 20 field values into a single `useRef` object and mutate it as the user types along
variants.rationale: The re-render cost comes from every keystroke updating shared state that the whole form subtree reads. You only need live behavior on email, so keep just that field controlled and let the rest be uncontrolled (read at submit) or move each field's state into its own small component so a keystroke re-renders only that field. Match the tool to each field's actual interactivity need.
optionExplanations: All-uncontrolled is fast but drops the live email validation the requirement explicitly keeps.
Correct — control only the field that needs live behavior and isolate or uncontrol the rest, so keystrokes don't re-render the whole form.
`React.memo` on the form itself can't stop re-renders caused by the form's own state changing; the state lives inside it.
Refs don't re-render, so a controlled email field reading from a ref couldn't validate live — this defeats the one requirement kept.
variants.interviewTip: Show you can mix strategies: 'controlled isn't all-or-nothing per form — I control the fields that need live behavior and isolate state so a keystroke re-renders one field, not twenty.'

sections.heading: Data fetching in effects: races and cleanup
paragraphs: When you fetch inside `useEffect(fn, [id])`, changing `id` starts a new request without cancelling the old one. Two requests are now in flight, and the network doesn't promise order — the slower, older one can resolve *after* the newer one and overwrite fresh data with stale. This is a race condition, and it's the most common effect-based bug in real apps.

The cleanup function is the fix. Capture a per-run flag — `let ignore = false` — and set `ignore = true` in cleanup; in the `.then`, bail if `ignore` is set so a superseded response can't call `setState`. Or use an `AbortController`: create one per run, pass its signal to `fetch`, and call `controller.abort()` in cleanup to actually cancel the request. Both guarantee only the latest run's result reaches state.

Don't forget the other states around the happy path: set a loading flag before the request, handle errors in a `.catch` (aborts throw an `AbortError` you should ignore), and remember StrictMode double-invokes the effect in development precisely to surface missing cleanup. For anything beyond trivial fetching, a data library (React Query, SWR) handles caching, dedup, and cancellation for you.
sections.summary: Async effects can race: a slow old request may resolve after a fast new one and clobber it — cancel or disown the previous run in cleanup with an `AbortController` or an `ignore` flag so only the latest response reaches state.

variants.question: A detail page fetches `/api/item/{id}` in an effect keyed on `id`. Clicking quickly through items sometimes leaves an older item's data on screen. What's the root cause?
options: Two fetches overlap and the slower older one resolves last, overwriting the newer response
The effect's dependency array is missing `id`, so it never refetches when the item changes
React caches the first fetch response and reuses it for every subsequent item id after that
`fetch` returns synchronously, so the second call blocks until the first has fully finished
variants.rationale: It's a race condition. Each `id` change fires a new request while the previous one is still in flight, and responses can arrive out of order — if the older request resolves last, its `setState` wins and shows stale data. The cleanup function must invalidate the prior run (an `ignore` flag or `AbortController`) so only the newest response commits.
optionExplanations: Correct — overlapping in-flight requests can resolve out of order, and the older one landing last overwrites the newer data.
The effect is keyed on `id`, so it does refetch; the problem is uncancelled overlap, not a missing dependency.
React doesn't cache `fetch` results on its own; each render's effect makes a real request.
`fetch` is asynchronous and returns a promise immediately, so calls overlap rather than blocking.
variants.interviewTip: Say 'race condition' explicitly, then the mechanism: 'responses aren't ordered, so a stale one can win — I disown the previous run in cleanup.' Naming the class of bug is half the credit.

variants.question: Which cleanup correctly prevents a superseded fetch from updating state in `useEffect(() => { fetch(url).then(r => r.json()).then(setData) }, [url])`?
options: Call `setData(null)` in the cleanup function so the stale response has nothing to overwrite
Set `let ignore = false`, flip it in cleanup, and skip `setData` when `ignore` is true
Add `data` to the dependency array so the effect re-runs until the response finally matches
Wrap `setData` in `useCallback` so only the newest handler identity is allowed to run
variants.rationale: A closure-scoped `let ignore = false`, set to `true` in the effect's cleanup, is captured by that run's `.then`; when `url` changes, cleanup fires, the old run's `ignore` becomes `true`, and its resolved `.then` sees the flag and skips `setData`. Only the current run's flag stays `false`, so only its response commits. (An `AbortController` is the alternative that also cancels the network work.)
optionExplanations: Clearing to `null` in cleanup doesn't stop the old request's `.then`, which still runs later and overwrites with stale data.
Correct — a per-run `ignore` flag flipped in cleanup lets the resolved-but-superseded request check the flag and decline to call `setData`.
Depending on `data` makes the effect loop after its own `setData` and does nothing to order the responses.
`setData` is already stable from `useState`; `useCallback` doesn't gate which response is allowed to land.
variants.interviewTip: Know both tools: 'the `ignore` flag prevents the stale `setState`; `AbortController` also cancels the request. Mentioning both — and that aborts throw `AbortError` to ignore — reads as senior.'

variants.question: A search box fires a fetch in an effect keyed on `query` — one request per keystroke. The server gets hammered and results flicker as responses land out of order. What's the best-practice combination?
options: Move the fetch out of the effect and into the `onChange` handler so React stops re-running it
Debounce the input and cancel the prior request in cleanup, so only the latest query resolves
Cache every response in a ref so repeated queries never actually hit the network again at all
Switch the effect to `useLayoutEffect` so each fetch finishes before the next keystroke fires
variants.rationale: Two problems stack here: too many requests, and out-of-order results. Debouncing the `query` (fire the effect only after typing pauses) cuts the request volume, and cleaning up each run — abort or `ignore` — ensures a late older response can't overwrite the newest. Together they give one settled result per intended query. A data library bakes both in.
optionExplanations: Moving the fetch to `onChange` doesn't reduce request count or fix ordering; you'd reimplement cleanup by hand and lose the effect's tie to `query`.
Correct — debouncing throttles the request volume and cleanup cancels or disowns superseded runs, so only the latest query's result lands.
A ref cache helps repeat queries but does nothing for the flood of new distinct queries or the out-of-order race.
`useLayoutEffect` changes timing relative to paint, not the ordering of async network responses, so the race remains.
variants.interviewTip: Layer the fixes: 'debounce to reduce requests, cleanup to defeat the race, and cache/dedup on top — which is exactly what React Query or SWR give you out of the box.'

variants.question: A developer uses `useEffect(async () => { const r = await fetch(url); setData(await r.json()) }, [url])` and gets a warning that an effect must not return a Promise. What's the correct structure?
options: Just return the async function's promise anyway; React will happily unwrap it and await the resolved result for you
Define an async function inside the effect and call it, so the effect itself returns cleanup or nothing
Replace `useEffect` with `useMemo`, which is the hook actually designed for asynchronous work
Mark the whole component `async` so its effects are permitted to await network calls directly
variants.rationale: An `async` function always returns a promise, but React expects an effect to return either nothing or a cleanup function — a returned promise would be mistaken for cleanup. Declare an async helper *inside* the effect and invoke it: `useEffect(() => { const load = async () => { ... }; load(); return () => {/* cleanup */}; }, [url])`. Now the effect returns a real cleanup, and the async work runs within it.
optionExplanations: React doesn't await effect return values — it calls them as cleanup, so returning a promise breaks the cleanup contract.
Correct — nesting the async function and calling it lets the effect return proper cleanup instead of a promise.
`useMemo` is for memoizing computed values during render, not for side effects or async fetching.
Components can't be `async`; rendering must be synchronous, so this doesn't address the effect's return type.
variants.interviewTip: State the contract: 'an effect returns cleanup or undefined, never a promise — so I put the `async` function inside and invoke it, keeping the return slot free for cleanup.'

sections.heading: useReducer for complex state
paragraphs: `useReducer` centralizes state transitions in one pure function: `(state, action) => newState`. Instead of scattering many `setX` calls across handlers, components `dispatch({ type: 'submit' })` and the reducer decides how the state changes. It shines when the next state depends on the previous one, when several values change together, or when the same transition fires from many places.

The signals to switch from `useState`: you have a cluster of related fields (form + validity + submission status), updates involve conditional logic ('if pending, ignore this action'), or you're passing five setters down through props. A reducer collapses those into a single `dispatch`, which is also referentially stable — handy to pass through context without re-creating callbacks.

Reducers must stay pure: compute and return a new state object, never mutate the argument, and don't do side effects (no fetches, no logging to a server) inside them — those belong in effects or event handlers. Because a reducer is a plain function of state and action, it's trivially unit-testable in isolation, without rendering anything.
sections.summary: Reach for `useReducer` when state transitions get complex or interrelated — it centralizes the logic in one pure, testable `(state, action) => newState` function and gives you a single stable `dispatch` instead of a fistful of setters.

variants.question: A component juggles `data`, `isLoading`, `error`, and `retryCount`, with handlers that update several of these together in coordinated ways. Which refactor fits best?
options: Model the transitions with `useReducer` so related fields update together in one place
Keep four separate `useState` calls and carefully update each one in every handler by hand
Store all four fields in a single `useRef` object and mutate them as events come in
Put the four fields on a global singleton so any component can update them from anywhere
variants.rationale: These four fields move together — starting a fetch sets `isLoading` true and clears `error`; success sets `data` and clears loading; failure sets `error` and bumps `retryCount`. A reducer expresses each transition as one atomic action, keeping the interrelated fields consistent and the logic in a single testable place, rather than remembering to update four independent states in every handler.
optionExplanations: Correct — coordinated multi-field transitions are exactly what a reducer centralizes into single atomic actions.
Four independent setters per handler is the error-prone status quo the reducer is meant to replace; it's easy to update one and forget another.
A ref doesn't trigger re-renders, so a loading/error UI built on it wouldn't update — wrong tool for view state.
A global singleton adds shared mutable state and re-render problems without solving the coordination; it's overkill and outside React's model.
variants.interviewTip: Name the trigger: 'when several pieces of state change together or the next state depends on the last, I reach for a reducer so transitions are atomic and testable.'

variants.question: A reducer case runs `state.items.push(action.item); return state;`. The list doesn't update on screen. What's wrong?
options: Reducers can't manage array state, so `items` must be lifted into its own separate `useState`
The action needs a unique `id` field, or React can't tell which dispatched action to apply
It mutated and returned the same state object, so React sees an unchanged reference and skips
`dispatch` has to be awaited before the pushed item will actually appear in the rendered list
variants.rationale: The same referential-equality rule that governs `useState` applies here: `push` mutates the existing array and the case returns the very same `state` object, so React's `Object.is` check sees no change and skips the render. A reducer must return a *new* state: `return { ...state, items: [...state.items, action.item] }`.
optionExplanations: Reducers handle arrays fine; the issue is mutation, not the state shape.
Actions don't need ids; the reducer runs synchronously for the dispatched action regardless.
Correct — mutating and returning the same object keeps the reference identical, so React bails out just as it does with `useState`.
`dispatch` isn't awaitable; the update is synchronous and would show immediately if a new reference were returned.
variants.interviewTip: Reinforce the through-line: 'immutability isn't a `useState` quirk — reducers must return new references too, or the `Object.is` bailout eats your update.'

variants.question: A `useState`-based form has grown to seven `setX` calls threaded down through three prop layers. Why is `useReducer` an appealing migration here beyond just tidiness?
options: A reducer runs its state updates on a background thread, so deep forms feel measurably faster
`dispatch` is stable across renders, so passing one function down beats threading seven changing setters
`useReducer` automatically persists form state to storage, which seven `useState` calls cannot do
Reducers re-render only the single changed field, whereas plain `useState` always re-renders the entire whole form tree
variants.rationale: `useReducer` returns a `dispatch` function that React guarantees is stable for the component's lifetime. Passing that single stable function down replaces threading seven separate setters (each a prop that can defeat memoization), and children just `dispatch` typed actions. That's a real structural win — fewer, more stable props and one place that owns the transition logic — not merely cosmetic.
optionExplanations: There's no background thread; reducers run synchronously on the main thread just like setters.
Correct — `dispatch` is referentially stable, so passing one function down is cleaner and more memo-friendly than seven changing setters.
`useReducer` has no built-in persistence; you'd still wire storage yourself in an effect.
Both hooks re-render the component that holds the state the same way; reducers don't grant per-field rendering.
variants.interviewTip: Highlight the stable dispatch: 'a reducer gives me one referentially-stable `dispatch` to pass through context or props, instead of a bundle of setters that churn references.'

variants.question: A developer puts `fetch('/log', ...)` and `analytics.track(...)` directly inside a reducer case so it 'runs on every action'. Why is this a problem?
options: Reducers execute only once at mount, so the side effects would never fire on later actions
Side effects belong in effects or handlers; reducers must stay pure and may be called twice
React throws a runtime error the moment any network call appears inside a reducer function
The `fetch` would block the reducer, freezing the UI until the network request came back
variants.rationale: Reducers must be pure functions of `(state, action)` — same inputs, same output, no side effects. React may call a reducer more than once for a single dispatch (StrictMode double-invokes it to catch impurity), so a `fetch` or analytics call inside it can fire twice or at unexpected times. Put side effects in event handlers or in an effect that responds to the resulting state change.
optionExplanations: Reducers run on every dispatched action, not just at mount; the frequency isn't the issue — the impurity is.
Correct — reducers must be pure and can be invoked twice (e.g. StrictMode), so side effects must live in handlers or effects instead.
React doesn't throw on a network call in a reducer; it just misbehaves silently, which is more dangerous than an error.
`fetch` is async and returns immediately, so it wouldn't block the reducer — the real problem is that it's an impure side effect.
variants.interviewTip: Keep the purity line bright: 'reducers compute the next state and nothing else — side effects go in handlers or effects, partly because StrictMode double-invokes reducers to catch exactly this.'
